Chapter 11 — Moderate Nonskeletal Problems
in Preadolescent Children: Preventive & Interceptive Treatment

Plain text is your original summary. Coloured items are 7th-edition additions/revisions; red marks important exceptions & cautions. Figures sit in the right margin (zoom to read the book caption inside each).
Treatment in Preadolescent Children — What Is Different?
  • Orthodontic treatment is rarely done in the primary dentition, for three reasons: (1) moving primary incisors/canines tends to cause accelerated root resorption; (2) moving primary teeth has little effect on where the permanent teeth erupt; (3) growth-modification effects in young children are lost to a resumption of the original growth pattern.
  • Primary-dentition treatment = "very early treatment." Preadolescence = mixed dentition = early / preventive & interceptive treatment.

Key points when early treatment is considered:

  • Goals must be clearly outlined. If mixed-dentition treatment runs too long: (1) patients get "burned out" before comprehensive treatment, and (2) the chance of damage to teeth/supporting structures rises.
  • Biomechanical differences exist between complete and partial appliances — the typical mixed-dentition fixed appliance is a "2 × 4" or "2 × 6".
  • Anchorage control is harder and more critical; implant-supported anchorage usually isn't practical (unerupted teeth, immature bone).
  • Beware unerupted teeth — don't tip lateral incisor roots into the path of erupting canines (→ lateral incisor root resorption).
  • Manage space closure carefully — unbanded/unbonded teeth get squeezed out of the arch.
  • Use interarch mechanics sparingly — Class II/III/vertical elastics are risky with partial appliances (exception: cross-elastics for unilateral crossbite).
  • If early treatment is in one arch only, the untreated arch dictates the final result.
  • Retention is often needed between mixed-dentition treatment and eruption of the permanent teeth; the transition from mixed to permanent dentition is a particularly unstable time, so overcorrection + careful retention matter.
Pretreatment Evaluation — Determining Complexity & Timing
Reframed The 6th edition called this Orthodontic Triage. The current edition frames it as "Orthodontic Pretreatment Evaluation" — same goal (sort moderate problems handled in general practice from complex ones to refer), with the generalist as the gatekeeper who must recognise problems and decide observe / treat / refer. (your summary said "Orthodontic Triage")

Step 1 Syndromes & Developmental Abnormalities

  • Separate out patients with facial syndromes or similarly complex problems.
  • Children developing above the 97th or below the 3rd percentile need special evaluation; significant skeletal asymmetry is always severe.
  • Complex medical treatments — radiation, bisphosphonates, and now growth hormones — can affect dentofacial development and treatment response.New
  • Missing primary teeth are very rare (0.5–0.9%) — usually a maxillary lateral incisor, and the permanent lateral is then also likely missing.New

Step 2 Facial Form Analysis

Updated Evaluate with the Facial Form Analysis method (your summary said "Facial Profile Analysis") — screen for AP (maxillary/mandibular protrusion-retrusion) and vertical (long-/short-face) discrepancies, plus lip protrusion/competence [method in Ch 6]Linked · Ch 6. A cephalogram is not required at this stage, but dental radiographs are (bitewings + anterior occlusal, or panoramic).
  • Skeletal Class II / Class III and the long-face / short-face types are complex.
  • Class II can be deferred to near adolescence (equally effective). Class III from moderate maxillary deficiency should be addressed earlierrefined; a protrusive-mandible Class III needs Class III elastics to skeletal anchorage in adolescence, or orthognathic surgery after growth.
  • Long-face/open-bite problems can improve with preadolescent treatment but be aggravated by growth into the late teens; short-face problems usually wait for comprehensive adolescent treatment unless a deep bite is causing palatal gingival damage.
  • Excessive dental protrusion/retrusion — urgency depends on esthetics or, for protrusion, trauma risk (a child <9 y with prior trauma has 8.4× the chance of additional trauma).

Step 3 Dental Development

  • Problems of dental development often need treatment as soon as discovered (early mixed dentition).
  • Asymmetric eruption (one side ahead by ≥6 months) is significant and usually needs early intervention; a few have a history of childhood head/neck radiation or trauma.
  • Missing/ankylosed permanent teeth (incl. primary failure of eruption) are complex.
    • For ankylosed primary teeth with successors, the permanent tooth usually erupts on time but may be malpositioned by a retained root tip.New
  • Supernumerary teeth — multiples suggest a syndrome (e.g. cleidocranial dysplasia). Ectopic eruption is another developmental problem.

Step 4 Space Problems

  • A space discrepancy of ~6 mm or more (with or without protrusion) is complex; if protrusion coexists, assume the natural limit of incisor advancement is reached. Severe crowding ≥10 mm needs complex planning and often early intervention so permanent teeth aren't impacted/deflected.

Step 5 Other Occlusal Discrepancies

  • A posterior crossbite in a preadolescent is moderate if there are no other complicating factors.
Management of Occlusal Relationship Problems

I. Posterior Crossbite

New Posterior crossbite was present in 7.1% of US children aged 8–11 (NHANES III) — usually from a narrow maxilla, often after prolonged sucking. Treat early if there is a CR–CO shift (centric-relation-to-centric-occlusion lateral shift). Timing matters because the transverse dimension is the first to finish growing.
  • Correct early if the child shifts on closure or constriction significantly reduces arch space; otherwise defer (before midpalatal suture bridging). Determine skeletal (correcting the skeletal discrepancy eliminates the crossbite) vs dental — early on, treatment is the same (light forces move teeth and bone).
  • A 1-mm increase in inter-premolar width adds ~0.7 mm of arch perimeter.
  • An expansion lingual arch is best at this age; heavy jackscrew force is only needed once the suture interdigitates in adolescence. Rapid expansion is not indicated in the primary/early mixed dentition (risk of nose distortion in young children).

Three approaches to moderate posterior crossbite:

  • 1. Equilibration (apparent crossbite) — if a shift is due solely to a primary-canine (or, less often, primary-molar) interference, limited equilibration (often just reducing the primary canines) eliminates it Fig 11.14.
  • 2. Expansion of a constricted maxilla. (If the first molars will erupt within 6 months, wait so correction includes them. If constriction is so great the maxillary teeth fit inside the mandibular teeth, there's no shift and less reason for early correction.)
    • Preferred: an adjustable lingual arch. The W-arch Fig 11.17 and quad helix Fig 11.18 are equivalent in force; the W-arch is opened 4–6 mm wider than passive; the quad helix's bulky helices also help stop a finger habit. Both leave a tongue imprint (up to a year to resolve).
    • Expand ~2 mm/month until slightly overcorrected (maxillary lingual cusps on the lingual inclines of the mandibular buccal cusps). Data: ~3.9 mm palatal and 6.5 mm intermolar expansion. Most need 2–3 months active + 3 months retention.
  • 3. Unilateral repositioning (true unilateral constriction) — asymmetric W-arch/quad-helix arms Fig 11.22, or a mandibular lingual arch with cross-elastics. Cross-elastics extrude posterior teeth — use with caution in increased lower-face-height or limited overbite.

II. Anterior Crossbite

  • Differentiate skeletal from dental — if truly skeletal, simply moving the incisor is inadequate. A crossbite of one or two teeth is almost always from lingually displaced maxillary incisors.
    • Central incisors can be deflected lingually by supernumerary anterior teeth or overretained primary incisors; because supernumerary lower incisors occur, count the teeth.New
  • Most common cause = lack of space. Correct dental anterior crossbites early because lingually positioned incisors limit excursions / cause incisal abrasion, and gingival recession is a risk (especially lower incisors).

Removable appliance

  • Fingersprings tip maxillary incisors facially. Place without a biteplate first (a biteplate risks over-eruption of teeth out of contact) — open the bite only if after 2 months opposing teeth move with the applied teeth (exception: very deep bite / bruxism).
  • Fingersprings activated 1.5–2 mm → ~1 mm/month. Slightly overcorrect; 1–2 months passive retention.

Fixed appliance

  • Simplest: a maxillary lingual arch with fingersprings ("whip springs") → ~1 mm/month. A 2 × 4 is best with crowding, rotation, need for bodily movement, or more teeth in crossbite.
  • Methods to advance aligned incisors: open-coil springs Fig 11.30 (archwire TMA/steel ≤18-mil in a 22-mil slot so it slides) or an "advanced" archwire with rolled-in loops mesial to the molars. A 2×4 in the lower arch can derotate/retract lower incisors causing the crossbite.New
  • Retention: a couple of months' wear; if rotations/spacing were also treated, a Hawley with a lateral-to-lateral labial bow (lets the laterals adjust as the canines erupt — an advantage over a bonded lingual retainer).New

III. Anterior Open Bite

  • An open bite with normal vertical proportions is usually a habit; a large lower-anterior-face-height + severe open bite = a skeletal (complex) problem.
  • Sucking effects (more in girls / non-breastfed): maxillary incisors tip facially, mandibular lingually, eruption impeded, often a narrowed maxilla → posterior crossbite + V-shaped arch. If the habit stops before the permanent incisors erupt, most changes self-correct — except the posterior crossbite. If the child doesn't want to quit, appliance therapy isn't indicated.
  • Most moderate open bites resolve by adolescence; with good skeletal proportions the open bite needs no other treatment once the habit stops.New

Habit-therapy ladder:

  • (1) discussion → (2) reminder → (3) reward → (4) elastic bandage loosely around the elbow at night (6–8 weeks). Commercial thumb covers / bitter nail preparations also work.
  • Appliance therapy (only if the above fail and the child wants to quit): a maxillary lingual arch with an anterior crib, effective in 85–90% (wire 38–40 mil). Leave it 6 months after the habit stops.

IV. Deep Bite

  • True reduced lower-face height is skeletal (complex). Under-eruption of posteriors / over-eruption of anteriors is also complex (comprehensive treatment) — rarely treated in the mixed dentition unless tissue damage is developing. Interim: a removable appliance with an anterior bite plane encourages posterior eruption and protects the tissue (temporary).
Management of Eruption Problems

I. Overretained Primary Teeth

  • Overretained primary maxillary molars usually keep a buccal or the large lingual root; mandibular ones a mesial or distal root. Incisors typically erupt lingually then move facially once the overretained primary tooth is shed/removed.

II. Ectopic Eruption

Three frequent patterns: lateral incisors (both arches), maxillary first molars, and maxillary canines.

Lateral incisors

  • Loss of one/both primary canines during lateral eruption signals a space shortage → eventual expansion or premolar extraction. Early loss of a maxillary primary canine rarely needs immediate treatment; a mandibular one can be more complex (incisor liability vs true arch-length shortage).
  • After losing one primary canine, a clinically significant midline shift was not greater than in normal eruption (1.3 vs 1.0 mm) — so it's not necessary to extract the contralateral canine or hold the midline; minor correction can be deferred.New evidence

Maxillary first molars

  • Diagnosed on bitewings. Small resorption (<1–1.5 mm) → watchful waiting (self-correction possible); if blocked eruption persists 6 months or resorption increases, treat.
  • Move the ectopic molar away from the primary molar it's resorbing: a 28-mil dead-soft brass wire (your summary said 22-mil)gauge updated looped around the contact and tightened ~2-weekly Fig 11.41, or a steel spring-clip separator. Elastomeric separators can dislodge apically — not recommended. If severe with occlusal access, a fixed appliance distalizes the molar; if the primary molar is destroyed, extract + place a distal shoe.

Maxillary canines

  • At ~age 10, if a primary canine isn't mobile and there's no facial bulge, suspect ectopic eruption — panoramic first, then small-FOV CBCT for root resorption and position. Risks: canine impaction and/or resorption of lateral/central incisor roots. If a mesial canine threatens resorption (not yet occurring), extract the primary canine.
  • Ericson & Kurol: if the canine crown overlaps < half the lateral root, 91% normalize after primary-canine extraction; if > half, 64%.
    • A systematic review confirms this, and extracting the primary canine with maxillary expansion encourages eruption even more.New
  • If incisor-root resorption is already occurring, surgically expose the canine and apply traction Fig 11.47.

Supernumerary · Delayed eruption · Ankylosed primary

  • Single supernumerary (commonest in the anterior maxilla) → early extraction (multiples → Ch 12). Delayed incisor eruption (no eruption >1 yr after normal, neighbours erupted) → treat; superficial tooth → soft-tissue excision; deeper → fixed-appliance traction (Ch 12).
  • Ankylosed primary tooth WITH successor — maintain until it interferes, then extract + lingual arch.
    • Ankylosed primary molar WITHOUT a successor: erupting teeth bring bone, so early extraction + space maintenance won't stop continued ridge resorption → this plan needs later bone grafting (full management in Ch 12).New
Space Analysis — Quantifying Space Problems

I. Principles

  • Crowding and protrusion are two aspects of the same phenomenon (teeth in equilibrium between tongue and lip forces). With a jaw discrepancy the dentition shifts — so space analysis is less accurate for skeletal problems.
  • Three assumptions: (1) incisor AP position is correct; (2) available space won't change from growth/tipping; (3) all teeth present and normal in size.

II. Estimating Unerupted Permanent Teeth

  • Two approaches: measure on radiographs (fair–good), or proportionality tables — lower-incisor size predicts upper canines/premolars best (upper laterals are highly variable) — the Tanaka–Johnston method.
New
  • Tanaka–Johnston does not include the potential mesial molar shift — add it if it matters (it shortens available space).
  • Factor the facial form analysis in — if incisors/lips should be proclined/retroclined for esthetics, that increases/decreases arch space.
  • Space analysis can also be done by a computer algorithm Fig 11.54.
Treatment of Space Problems

I. Premature Tooth Loss With Adequate Space — Space Maintenance

  • Appropriate only with adequate space, and unnecessary if a successor will erupt within 6 months (≥½–⅔ root).
  • Also inappropriate if the child is non-compliant, or has poor oral hygiene / high caries.New
  • Band-and-loop Fig 11.55 — unilateral. Before the permanent incisors erupt, a single primary molar lost bilaterally → a pair of band-and-loops rather than a lingual arch (incisor buds erupt lingually).
  • Partial-denture maintainer — bilateral posterior loss of >1 tooth/segment before the incisors erupt; restores some function. (Anterior space maintenance is generally unnecessary.)
  • Distal shoe Fig 11.57 — primary second molar lost before the permanent first molar erupts; guide plane ~1 mm below the mesial marginal ridge.
  • Lingual arch Fig 11.58 — multiple missing posteriors once the incisors have erupted; rest on the cingula ~1–1.5 mm off tissue. Maxillary lingual arches are contraindicated when bite depth makes the lower incisors hit the wire — then use a Nance or transpalatal arch.

II. Localized Space Loss (≤3 mm) — Space Regaining

  • Up to 3 mm can be regained locally. Maxillary: distal tipping + derotation of molars regains 2–3 mm; a removable appliance with Adams clasps + helical fingerspring is ideal for tipping one molar (activate ~2 mm → 1 mm/month) Fig 11.60; for bodily movement use fixed.
  • Mandibular: removable appliances are less satisfactory — prefer fixed. For bilateral loss from lingual incisor tipping, use a lip bumper Fig 11.63 or an adjustable lingual arch (a lip bumper is not a space maintainer; a lingual arch can stay as one).

III. Mild Crowding  ·  IV. Space Management (Leeway)  ·  V. Generalized Crowding

  • Incisor liability causes transient crowding — up to 2 mm can resolve spontaneously. Disking primary canines/first molars can gain 3–4 mm (but teeth may align more lingually) Fig 11.65 — mainly for esthetics.
  • Leeway space = 2.5 mm per side mandible, 1.5 mm per side maxilla. Much of a deficiency is the allowance for mesial molar drift to Class I — prevent that drift and there's little/no deficiency.
  • Gianelly: ~75% of patients (Boston University) would have roughly enough space if molar drift were prevented — little, easy treatment.New
  • For moderate crowding with little/no discrepancy, begin a lingual arch in the late mixed dentition, just before the second primary molars exfoliate. Because the molars are held back, they often stay end-to-end → correcting the molar relationship becomes a goal.
  • Generalized 2–4 mm discrepancy → plan arch expansion (mandible: adjustable lingual arch; maxilla: removable or fixed), unless incisors are severely protrusive.

VI. Other Tooth Displacements

  • Spaced & flared maxillary incisors (often post-thumb-sucking) — eliminate the habit first, then a Hawley with clasps + labial bow. A deep overbite must be corrected before retracting upper incisors.
  • Maxillary midline diastema — in the "ugly duckling" stage diastemas tend to close spontaneously; a small (≤2 mm) one can be closed by tipping the centrals (removable, esthetics only). A diastema >2 mm → suspect a midline supernumerary/lesion; needs bodily movement + retention (Ch 12).
